in_text_mentions: ent was discharged on empiric antibiotic treatment for presumed otitis media. The patient represented to care two days later with worsening purpuric and tender rash which had spread to his left upper extremity and bilateral lower extremities (Figures 1, 2). He stated he had a similar rash approximately one year prior which resolved without medical intervention. The rash also showed no signs of blanching. The leading differential diagnosis became a vasculitis of unknown etiology, possibly rheumatoid arthritis given the history of autoimmune disease, and the patient was discharged on prednisone.

plate_findings.evidence: bilateral scarlet-colored purpura that was contiguous and non-blanching (Figure 1). It covered his inner thighs

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Caption 'Levamisole-induced vasculitis' panels A-D with purpuric lesions; in-text describes contiguous non-blanching scarlet purpura of inner thighs matching visual retiform purpura in panel A. B: Caption attributes panels to levamisole-induced vasculitis; visual shows scattered purpuric violaceous lesions down leg consistent with retiform purpura of extremities. C: Same disease attribution as panels A-B; large confluent scarlet to deep purple non-blanching purpura of thigh/leg typical of levamisole vasculopathy retiform purpura. D: Caption includes panel D as levamisole-induced vasculitis lesion on flank; in-text notes purpura covered left flank; morphology is purpuric retiform plaque, vocabulary has only extremity retiform purpura term so coded by morphology with trunk site in proposed term.
panels.attribution_text: Latif et al. Levamisole-induced Vasculitis in a Hepatitis C Patient: A General Medicine Ward Perspective on Diagnosis and Management.. Cureus 2019. doi:10.7759/cureus.5198. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Levamisole-induced vasculitis in a cocaine user. Images obtained one week after cocaine use. Black arrows pointing to lesions scattered across his body shown in panels A, B, C, and D.
in_text_mentions: saturation was 97% on room air. The physical exam was significant for coarse breath sounds bilaterally. He was coughing throughout the exam, with a small amount of bloody sputum production. He had bilateral scarlet-colored purpura that was contiguous and non-blanching (Figure 1). It covered his inner thighs and left flank. The purpura extended down both thighs, with deep purple lesions scattered throughout. Lesions were not raised, no skin breakdown could be appreciated, and some lesions were surrounded by hyperpigmented rings. He had mild erythema across the anterior abdomen and right flank.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a real patient (39-year-old woman with crack cocaine use and hepatitis C) showing dry gangrene/necrotic eschar of the right hand, a recognized manifestation of levamisole-induced vasculopathy in an article specifically titled 'Levamisole-Induced Vasculitis.' Attribution and findings are well supported. B: Clinical photograph of the same patient showing violaceous purpuric plaques with necrosis/gangrene of the cheeks and nasal tip, a classic facial manifestation of levamisole-induced vasculopathy. Attribution is supported by the article title and the specific captioned lesions.

Physical examination revealed dry necrotic tissue over the dorsum of her right hand and right ring and small fingers, with the absence of sensation to touch over these regions. panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real patient's left hand showing well-demarcated dry gangrene (black necrotic eschar) of two digits, with arrows marking the affected digits and a ruler for scale. The article is specifically about cocaine-associated levamisole-induced vasculitis, and the in-text and caption directly attribute the gangrene to the patient's presentation, supporting attribution to levamisole vasculopathy. Digital gangrene with eschar fits the necrotic ulcers/eschar finding; it is a recognized severe rather than textbook presentation, hence variant typicality. Skin appears dark on visible, adequately lit unaffected skin. No ethnicity or age stated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Genuine human renal biopsy (PAS, 400x) from the patient diagnosed with systemic levamisole-induced vasculitis (article title and in-text pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis). Shows a glomerulus with proliferative glomerulonephritis surrounded by a cellular crescent, a recognized renal manifestation of the vasculopathy. Crescentic GN is not in the provided vocabulary, so it is listed as a proposed finding. B: Genuine human renal biopsy (H&E, 400x) from the levamisole-induced vasculitis patient. Caption describes a focus of fibrinoid necrosis with inflammation from necrotizing arteritis, corresponding to the vasculitic (fibrinoid necrosis) histology finding; the article's diagnosis is levamisole vasculopathy, so attribution is direct.
panels.attribution_text: Baptiste et al. Systemic Levamisole-Induced Vasculitis in a Cocaine User without Cutaneous Findings: A Consideration in Diagnosis.. Case reports in medicine 2015. doi:10.1155/2015/547023. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Renal biopsy. (a) PAS at 400x. Glomerulus showing proliferative glomerulonephritis surrounded by a cellular crescent. (b) H&E at 400x. Focus of fibrinoid necrosis with inflammation from necrotizing arteritis. PAS: periodic acid-Schiff-diastase; H&E: hematoxylin and eosin.
in_text_mentions: patitis B and C serologies were negative. There were no abnormal bands on serum or urine protein electrophoresis. ANCA were strongly positive at 1 : 5120 (upper limit of normal is less than 1 : 20) with a perinuclear staining pattern and myeloperoxidase reactivity at 76 AU/mls (upper limit of normal is less than 19 AU/mls). Kidney biopsy specimen had a total of 21 glomeruli, out of which only two were globally sclerotic. The majority of glomeruli showed pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis (Figure 1). A prominent plasma cell-rich tubulointerstitial nephritis was also present.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Nasal endoscopy patient image from article titled Cocaine- and Levamisole-Induced Vasculitis. Caption describes large hard- and soft-palate defect and cluster of three ulcerated lesions of posterior nasopharyngeal wall. In-text links Figure 3 to hard/soft palate perforations and pharyngeal wall ulcerations in this disease spectrum. No vocabulary finding_key covers mucosal destructive lesions, so recorded as proposed_findings. B: Endoscopic view from oral cavity in same patient showing anterior hard-palate fistula and larger hard- and soft-palate defect. Caption-specific manifestation plus disease-focused article title and in-text attribution of palate perforations to Figure 3 support levamisole_vasculopathy. No skin vocabulary term applies, so captured in proposed_findings.
panels.attribution_text: Iorio et al. Cocaine- and Levamisole-Induced Vasculitis: Defining the Spectrum of Autoimmune Manifestations.. Journal of clinical medicine 2024. doi:10.3390/jcm13175116. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Nasal endoscopy with a 30-degree endoscope shows a large hard- and soft-palate defect with evidence of oral cavity and laryngopharyngeal structures such as oral tongue, base of the tongue with hypertrophic lingual tonsils, free margin of the epiglottis, laryngeal vestibule, arytenoids, and retrocricoid space. A cluster of three ulcerated lesions of the posterior wall of the nasopharynx is visible. (B) Endoscopic view with a 30-degree endoscope from the oral cavity in the same patient revealed an anterior hard-palate fistula, and a larger hard- and soft-palate defect.
in_text_mentions: The most common signs, detectable by nasal endoscopy, are diffuse necrotizing ulcerative lesions, extensive crusting and nasal septal perforation. In more severe cases, external features like nasal deformity, saddle nose, loss of nasal projection, hard and/or soft palate perforations, erosion of middle and superior turbinate and sphenoid bone erosion may be observed (Figure 2 and Figure 3) [10].

Other rare manifestations include pharyngeal wall ulcerations (Figure 3) [64,65], nasolacrimal duct obstruction and destruction of the orbital bony walls, which can lead to secondary orbital cellulitis [66]. In these cases, damage could range from dehiscence of the lamina papyracea or of the orbital floor without visual symptoms to more severe conditions, such as chronic orbital inflammation, double vision, reduced visual acuity, ocular motility impairment, pseudotumor and optic neuropathy. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photo of earlobe purpura with central necrosis, a classic manifestation of levamisole-induced vasculitis per caption. B: Second earlobe photo showing purpuric necrotic lesions consistent with levamisole-induced vasculitis. C: Clinical photo of purpuric lesions on digits of the left upper extremity attributed to levamisole-induced vasculitis in caption. D: Clinical photo of purpuric necrotic lesion on the elbow from the same levamisole vasculitis case.
